prompt: An EC2 instance wears the role `shop-app` through its profile. An old script also left `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in the machine's environment. Which credentials does the AWS command line on that machine sign with?
hint: The chain stops at the first answer.

choices.text: The role's, because a role always takes precedence over a key
choices.why: Nothing ranks a role above a key. The order of the chain decides, and the metadata provider is the last one in it.

choices.text: The key in the environment
choices.why: Right. `env` is the first provider and it answered, so the chain never reached `iam-role`. The machine now acts as whoever owns that key, silently.

choices.text: Neither: the command line refuses when two providers disagree
choices.why: The chain never compares providers. It takes the first that answers and does not look further.

choices.text: Both, merged into a single session
choices.why: A request is signed with one set of credentials. There is no merging of two identities.

prompt: Put these providers in the order AWS CLI 2.37.4 tried them in the lesson's `--debug` output.
hint: Typed keys first, the network last.
trap: `container-role` sits just before `iam-role`, and the file in your home directory comes well before both.

prompt: `aws configure list` shows `iam-role` in the `TYPE` column and nothing under `LOCATION`. Where did the credentials come from?
hint: There is no file to name.

choices.text: From `~/.aws/credentials`, under a profile called `iam-role`
choices.why: That provider is `shared-credentials-file`, and it names the file it read in `LOCATION`.

choices.text: From `AWS_ROLE_ARN` in the environment
choices.why: `AWS_ROLE_ARN` with a token file is the web identity provider, which `configure list` reports as `assume-role-with-web-identity`.

choices.text: From the instance metadata service, over HTTP
choices.why: Right. `iam-role` is botocore's name for the metadata provider; the credentials arrived in an HTTP answer, so there is no location to show.

choices.text: From the role's own access key, created when the role was
choices.why: A role has no access key of its own. Whoever assumes it receives temporary credentials, which is the point of a role.

prompt: What does IMDSv2 ask for that IMDSv1 does not?
hint: Count the requests before the first answer.

choices.text: An access key, signed into every request to the service
choices.why: Nothing at the metadata address is signed. The instance has no key yet; that is what it is asking for.

choices.text: A token from a `PUT`, sent with every read
choices.why: Right. The `PUT` carries a header with the token's lifetime, and every `GET` after it carries the token.

choices.text: HTTPS instead of plain HTTP
choices.why: Both versions answer plain HTTP on `169.254.169.254`. The difference is the token, not the transport.

choices.text: The name of the role, given in the path
choices.why: Both versions put the role's name in the path, and both answer it when asked for the list.

prompt: On an EC2 instance, the metadata service answers at `http://___/`.
hint: A link-local address, the same on every instance.

prompt: On a laptop with no credentials anywhere, `aws s3 ls` waits a moment before saying `Unable to locate credentials`. Why the wait?
hint: Which provider is not a file or a variable?

choices.text: It asks AWS whether an account exists for this computer
choices.why: No provider asks AWS about the computer. Without credentials there is nothing to ask with.

choices.text: It retries `env` until the variables appear
choices.why: Each provider is tried once. The environment is read in an instant and found empty.

choices.text: The last provider sends requests to the metadata address and waits for a reply that never comes
choices.why: Right. `iam-role` makes network requests, and off EC2 nothing answers at `169.254.169.254`, so it waits for its timeout.

choices.text: It downloads the list of providers before trying them
choices.why: The order is built into botocore, which is inside the command line. Nothing is downloaded.

prompt: What does `run-instances` take to give a new instance the permissions of the role `shop-app`?
hint: The console hides a step the command line does not.

choices.text: The role's ARN, passed as `--role-arn`
choices.why: `run-instances` has no such option. A role reaches an instance inside a profile.

choices.text: An access key of the role, written into user data
choices.why: A role has no key, and a key in user data is a key anybody on the machine can read. Nothing in this lesson writes one.

choices.text: An instance profile that holds the role
choices.why: Right. `--iam-instance-profile Name=shop-app` names the profile, and the profile holds exactly one role.

choices.text: Nothing: every instance may assume every role whose name it knows
choices.why: A role's trust policy decides who may assume it, and an instance gets only the role in its profile.

prompt: Which principal does the trust policy of a role for EC2 instances name?
hint: The service that will assume it.

choices.text: The instance's id, such as `i-0ee42130b0c3e009d`
choices.why: An instance id is not a principal. The id appears later, as the session name when the role is assumed.

choices.text: `{"Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com"}`
choices.why: Right. EC2 assumes the role on the instance's behalf, so the service is the principal.

choices.text: The account root, so that every instance in it qualifies
choices.why: Naming the account trusts its users and roles, not EC2. An instance would still have nothing to assume it with.

choices.text: The instance profile's ARN
choices.why: The profile is a container for the role, not a principal that assumes it.

prompt: `bia` may call `ec2:RunInstances`. Launching with `--iam-instance-profile Name=shop-app` fails with `AccessDenied`. What is she missing?
hint: Handing a role to a machine is its own permission.

choices.text: `sts:AssumeRole` on `shop-app`
choices.why: She is not assuming the role; EC2 is. What she does is hand it over, and that needs a different permission.

choices.text: `ec2:AssociateIamInstanceProfile`, which every launch with a profile also calls
choices.why: That action replaces or adds a profile on an existing instance. A launch with a profile is checked for something else.

choices.text: `iam:PassRole` on the role `shop-app`
choices.why: Right. Without it anyone who may start machines could start one wearing the account's most powerful role.

prompt: Which of these are rules of IMDSv2, as AWS documents it? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three of the five are in the section's list.

choices.text: A read needs a token obtained with a `PUT` and a custom header
choices.why: Right. A request forged through a URL parameter is usually a `GET` and cannot add the header.

choices.text: A `PUT` carrying `X-Forwarded-For` gets no token
choices.why: Right. That header is the mark of a proxy, so a proxy on the instance cannot fetch a token for somebody else.

choices.text: The token's answer leaves with an IP time-to-live equal to the hop limit
choices.why: Right. With the default of 1 it dies after one hop and never reaches anything behind another network device.

choices.text: The credentials come back encrypted with the instance's own key
choices.why: They come back in plain JSON, which is why who may ask is the whole defence.

choices.text: Applications on the instance can no longer read the metadata
choices.why: They can, with a token. The SDK on the instance does the `PUT` itself, as the lesson's `--debug` showed.

prompt: After launching with `HttpTokens=required`, a plain `curl` with no token to moto's metadata address answers `200`. What does that measurement establish?
hint: Separate what moto stores from what moto enforces.

choices.text: That `HttpTokens=required` does not take effect until the instance restarts
choices.why: There is no instance to restart in moto, and on AWS the setting applies at launch. The cause is moto's imitation.

choices.text: That the token is optional on AWS too, whatever the setting says
choices.why: A result in moto proves nothing about AWS. AWS documents a `401 Unauthorized` for exactly this request.

choices.text: That `curl` sent a token without being asked to
choices.why: `curl` sends only the headers it is given, and none was given.

choices.text: Only that moto records the setting without enforcing it
choices.why: Right. `describe-instances` shows `required`, and moto's metadata service ignores it. What AWS refuses has to come from its documentation.

prompt: Two machines: an EKS node, whose pods must NOT use the node's role, and a single instance running the shop's app in Docker, which SHOULD use the instance's role. Which hop limits fit?
hint: A container on a bridge is one hop further than the instance.

choices.text: 1 on the node, 2 on the Docker instance
choices.why: Right. At 1 the token dies before reaching a pod; at 2 it reaches a container on the bridge.

choices.text: 2 on the node, 1 on the Docker instance
choices.why: That is the reverse: the pods would reach the node's role, and the container would not reach the one it needs.

choices.text: 1 on both, since a higher limit is never safe
choices.why: At 1 the shop's container gets no token and cannot use the role it was meant to use.

choices.text: 2 on both, since containers are a hop away in each case
choices.why: On the node, reaching the role is exactly what should fail, so the extra hop is the hole.

prompt: How many roles may one instance profile hold? moto refused the next one with `LimitExceeded`.
hint: The quota named in the error.

prompt: In an IRSA trust policy, what does the condition on `...:sub` restrict?
hint: Read the value: `system:serviceaccount:shop:checkout`.

choices.text: Which cluster may issue tokens for the role
choices.why: The issuer is the `Federated` principal, the registered provider. `sub` is about the workload inside it.

choices.text: Which service account, in which namespace, may assume the role
choices.why: Right. Without it every pod of the cluster holding a token could become the role.

choices.text: Who the token is meant for, which for IRSA is STS
choices.why: That is `aud`, the other condition. The two are separate checks on separate claims.

choices.text: How long the credentials returned may last
choices.why: Duration is a setting of the role and the request. A trust policy condition decides who, not how long.

prompt: Why is `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` sent without a signature?
hint: What does the pod hold before the call?

choices.text: Because STS is a global service and accepts unsigned calls from anyone
choices.why: Almost every STS call is signed, `AssumeRole` included. This one is the exception, for a reason that belongs to it.

choices.text: The pod has no AWS credential yet; the signed token is the proof
choices.why: Right. The cluster signed the token, and STS checks that signature instead of an AWS one.

choices.text: Because the role's trust policy turns signing off
choices.why: A trust policy decides who may assume the role. It has no say in how a request is sent.

choices.text: To save time, since pods start often
choices.why: Signing costs microseconds. The reason is that there is nothing to sign with.

prompt: In the lab, a token for `system:serviceaccount:other:intruder` got credentials for `shop-checkout`, whose trust policy names only `shop:checkout`. What should a reader conclude?
hint: Which part of the lesson was measured, and which was read?

choices.text: That `StringEquals` compares only the start of the value
choices.why: `StringEquals` is an exact comparison. The cause is that moto never evaluated it.

choices.text: That AWS lets any token in until the provider is verified
choices.why: AWS refuses such a token at the trust policy with `AccessDenied`. The lab says nothing about AWS here.

choices.text: That moto checks nothing about web identity, so the refusal is AWS's documented behaviour
choices.why: Right. It even accepted a role that does not exist. The lab shows how the credentials travel; what STS refuses comes from AWS's documentation.

choices.text: That the `sub` condition belongs in the role's permission policy instead
choices.why: Who may assume a role is the trust policy's question, and that is where the condition goes.

prompt: Match each way of giving a workload a role to the principal its trust policy names.
hint: Three services and one registered provider.

prompt: The shop runs three EKS clusters and wants one role, `shop-checkout`, usable by the checkout in all of them. Why does Pod Identity make that simpler than IRSA?
hint: Count what each cluster adds to the trust policy.

choices.text: Pod Identity credentials never expire, so nothing has to be renewed across clusters
choices.why: They expire like every temporary credential. The simplification is in the trust policy, not the lifetime.

choices.text: Pod Identity puts the clusters in one account automatically
choices.why: Pod Identity does not move clusters between accounts. The three were already in one.

choices.text: Its trust names one service principal, the same in every cluster
choices.why: Right. With IRSA each cluster is another provider to register and another condition in the trust policy.

choices.text: IRSA forbids a role being assumed from more than one cluster
choices.why: It allows it, with one `Federated` principal and condition per cluster. It is more to write, not forbidden.

prompt: On ECS, the agent serves a task role's credentials at `169.254.170.___`, and the container finds the path in `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_RELATIVE_URI`.
hint: Not the Pod Identity agent's address.

prompt: The shop's deploy pipeline runs on a CI service that issues each job a signed OIDC token. Which arrangement from this lesson lets it deploy with no stored AWS key?
hint: The CI service is an issuer, like a cluster.

choices.text: An instance profile on the CI service's machines
choices.why: Those machines are not in the shop's account, so the shop cannot give them a profile.

choices.text: Register the CI's issuer as an OIDC provider and let `deployer` trust it, with a `sub` condition naming the repository
choices.why: Right. It is IRSA's mechanism with a different issuer: the job's token is traded for `deployer` through `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`.

choices.text: Store a key as a CI secret and rotate it every month
choices.why: That is a stored key, which the question rules out. Lesson 12 treats it as the last resort.

choices.text: Point `AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI` at the CI service
choices.why: The container provider reads credentials somebody already holds. The CI service holds a token, not AWS credentials.

prompt: Put the steps of IRSA at run time in order, from a pod starting to its first call to S3.
hint: The token exists before anyone checks it.
items: the cluster writes a signed token into the pod's file
the SDK calls `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` with the token
STS verifies the signature with the issuer's keys
STS evaluates the trust policy's `sub` and `aud`
the pod signs a call to S3 with the credentials
trap: A trust policy is evaluated only for a token whose signature has already been verified.

prompt: A review finds an SSRF in the shop's image preview, on an instance where IMDSv1 is still on. Which change closes the path to the role's credentials?
hint: The forged request is a plain GET.

choices.text: A security group rule refusing traffic to `169.254.169.254`
choices.why: Security groups filter the instance's network interface, and the metadata service is reached without crossing them.

choices.text: Delete the instance profile
choices.why: That removes the credentials from the attacker and from the shop's app alike, which then cannot read `shop-assets`.

choices.text: `modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required`, then fix the preview
choices.why: Right. With tokens required a plain `GET` gets a `401`, and the SSRF itself still deserves its own fix.

choices.text: Rotate the access key in `~/.aws/credentials` on the instance
choices.why: An instance with a profile has no such key. The credentials at risk come from the metadata service.
